title: Describing things
goal: Describe people and things by colour, size and quality, make adjectives agree, and compare (bigger, the biggest).
intro:
Pashto adjectives **agree** with their noun in gender, number and case, so 'white' is سپين with a masculine noun but سپينه with a feminine one. A handful of very common adjectives are irregular (سور 'red' → سره), so it's worth learning the feminine form with each adjective.

Comparison, on the other hand, is easy: Pashto has no '-er' or '-est' endings. You just say 'this is big **than** that' (تر …) or 'big **than all**' (تر ټولو).

grammar.title: Adjective agreement
grammar.body:
Adjectives come **before** the noun (سپين موټر 'a white car') or after it with the verb 'to be' (موټر سپين دی 'the car is white'). Either way they agree with the noun.

**Type 1 — ending in a consonant** (most adjectives): add **-a** for feminine, **-e** for feminine plural; masculine plural is unchanged.
سپين موټر · سپين موټر (pl) · سپينه خولۍ · سپينې خولۍ

**Type 2 — ending in unstressed -ay**: masculine plural **-i**, feminine **-e** (singular and plural).
ښکلی هلک · ښکلي هلکان · ښکلې نجلۍ · ښکلې نجونې

**Irregular** (very common!): سور/سره (red), شين/شنه (green), زوړ/زړه (old), سوړ/سړه (cold), دروند/درنه (heavy), لوی/لويه (big).

**Invariable**: adjectives ending in -i (نسواري، آسماني) and a few others like ښايسته, خوشاله never change.

In the oblique plural all adjectives end in -o, just like nouns: د ښکلو نجونو 'of the beautiful girls'.

examples.en: an old house and an old tree

examples.note: شنه چای is the fixed name for green tea, and تور چای for black tea.

grammar.title: Comparison: تر … 'than' and تر ټولو 'most'
grammar.body:
Pashto adjectives have no comparative or superlative endings. To compare, put **تر** (tər) before the thing you are comparing with: 'A **than** B big is' — احمد **تر** محمود اوږد دی 'Ahmad is taller than Mahmood'. You can add ډېر or زيات 'more' for emphasis: تر هغه ډېر ښه 'much better than that'. **له … نه** is also used: له ما نه مشر دی 'he's older than me'.

For the **superlative**, compare with 'all': **تر ټولو** (tər ṭolo, 'than all') — تر ټولو لوی 'the biggest'.

The pronoun after تر goes into the oblique: تر ما 'than me', تر تا 'than you', تر هغه 'than him'.

dialogue.title: Which house is yours?
dialogue.setting: Mina shows her friend Spogmai a photo of her village in Swat.

lines.speaker: Spogmai
lines.native: واه، دا ډېر ښکلی ځای دی! دا لوړ غرونه چېرته دي؟
lines.roman: wāh, dā ḍer ṣkə́lay dzāy day! dā lwaṛ ġrúna chérta di?
lines.en: Wow, this is a very beautiful place! Where are these high mountains?

lines.speaker: Mina
lines.native: دا په سوات کې زموږ کلی دی.
lines.roman: dā pə swāt ke zmuẓ kə́lay day.
lines.en: This is our village in Swat.

lines.speaker: Spogmai
lines.native: ستاسو کور کوم يو دی؟ دا لوی سپين کور؟
lines.roman: stāso kor kum yaw day? dā loy spin kor?
lines.en: Which one is your house? This big white house?

lines.speaker: Mina
lines.native: نه، هغه زموږ د تره کور دی. زموږ کور تر هغه وړوکی دی.
lines.roman: na, haġá zmuẓ də trə kor day. zmuẓ kor tər haġə́ waṛúkay day.
lines.en: No, that's my uncle's house. Our house is smaller than that.

lines.speaker: Spogmai
lines.native: دا وړوکی کور چې شنه دروازه لري؟
lines.roman: dā waṛúkay kor che shna darwā́za lári?
lines.en: This little house with the green door?

lines.speaker: Mina
lines.native: هو! زوړ کور دی، خو ډېر ښکلی دی.
lines.roman: ho! zoṛ kor day, xo ḍer ṣkə́lay day.
lines.en: Yes! It's an old house, but it's very lovely.

lines.speaker: Mina
lines.native: دا زموږ د کلي تر ټولو زړه ونه ده.
lines.roman: dā zmuẓ də kə́li tər ṭolo zaṛá wə́na da.
lines.en: That's the oldest tree in our village.

lines.speaker: Spogmai
lines.native: سوات تر پېښور ډېر ښکلی دی!
lines.roman: swāt tər peṣawár ḍer ṣkə́lay day!
lines.en: Swat is much more beautiful than Peshawar!

culture: Pashto has rich vocabulary for appearance and character, and compliments are given freely about places, food and hospitality — but direct praise of a child or a person's looks is traditionally softened with **ماشاالله** to ward off the 'evil eye' (نظر). Colours carry associations: white is purity and peace (and the colour of mourning clothes in some areas), red and green appear in wedding clothes, and the black-red-green of the Afghan flag is a strong national symbol. Note that شين covers both green and blue — Pashtuns say a 'شين' sky and 'شين' grass, as many languages do.
